newsitem.title: INDIA: India's Hindu nationalists beaten in key bastion.
newsitem.headline: India's Hindu nationalists beaten in key bastion.

text.p: Hindu nationalists on Friday fell well short of their goal of winning an outright majority in elections in India's most populous state and suffered a blow in their efforts to win national power.
But the nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) retained enough clout to stir trouble between Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's coalition and its key backer, the Congress party, analysts said.

With results in all but one of the 425 seats in the state assembly declared, the BJP had won only 177 seats in Uttar Pradesh, considered the Hindu nationalists' political springboard for capturing power in New Delhi.

"It (the result) has dealt a stunning psychological blow to the party's long-term plans of becoming the national alternative to the Congress," executive editor Ajoy Bose wrote in The Pioneer newspaper on Friday.
The BJP, which built its national foundations on a Hindu revivalist agenda in Uttar Pradesh in the late 1980s, had hoped to win control of the country's biggest electoral prize.
The north Indian state wields enormous influence in the federal parliament where it has the largest number of seats.
Deve Gowda's United Front alliance finished second in the race with 134 seats.
Congress, which has ruled India for all but four years since independence in 1947, came in third as a junior partner in an alliance with the low-caste Bahujan Samaj Party (BSP).
But the Congress-BSP alliance, which won 100 seats, was standing firm by a demand that it be allowed to form the Uttar Pradesh government.
The Congress party says the United Front must support the team under BSP leader Mayawati in Uttar Pradesh in exchange for Congress' support in New Delhi.
Deve Gowda's minority coalition in the federal parliament would fall if Congress withdrew its support.

"If the United Front is really committed to driving out communal forces, then why are they hesitating in coming forward to extend support to a Mayawati-led Congress-BSP government?" Jitendra Prasada, Congress state party chief, told Reuters in the Uttar Pradesh capital Lucknow.
The BJP's rivals consider the party "communal" because they say it discriminates against the Moslem minority.

But the United Front was slow to take up Congress's demand because the party which won the most seats for Deve Gowda's coalition, the Samajwadi Party, is bitterly opposed to Mayawati. The feud is linked to India's complex Hindu caste hierarchy.

Samajwadi leader Mulayam Singh Yadav, who is Deve Gowda's defence minister, is backed by peasant caste farmers. Mayawati's Dalit, or former untouchable, supporters often work on their lands. The two formed a coalition in 1993, but later fell out.
Communications Minister Beni Prasad Varma, one of Yadav's key aides, minced no words as he threatened to rattle Deve Gowda's coalition if it backed the BSP.
"Any attempt to weaken Mulayam Singh Yadav will not be tolerated. If it comes to that, we will not hesitate to sever ties with the government in Delhi," Varma said on Wednesday.
In a thinly veiled attempt to drive a wedge between its rivals, the BJP offered to support Mayawati if it could join the government.
